claim: BAI1 loss from mouse or rat hippocampal neurons causes dendritic hypertrophy.
source: BAI1 loss from mouse or rat hippocampal neurons causes dendritic hypertrophy, whereas BAI1 overexpression precipitates dendrite retraction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased dendrite length, number, and branch points in BAI1 knockdown neurons in culture and in vivo (Figures 1-2).

claim: BAI1 overexpression precipitates dendrite retraction.
source: BAI1 loss from mouse or rat hippocampal neurons causes dendritic hypertrophy, whereas BAI1 overexpression precipitates dendrite retraction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing decreased dendrite length, number, and branch points in BAI1 overexpressing neurons (Figure 2f-l).

claim: BAI1-mediated dendritic growth defects specifically manifest as dendrites transition from growth to stability.
source: These defects specifically manifest as dendrites transition from growth to stability.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal imaging data showing that BAI1 Kd neurons continue growing after control neurons stop at 17 DIV (Figure 2a-e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: BAI1-mediated growth arrest is independent of its Rac1-dependent synaptogenic function.
source: BAI1-mediated growth arrest is independent of its Rac1-dependent synaptogenic function.
evidence: Supported by data showing that the BAI1•∆TEV mutant rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits (Figure 5a,f-h, Duman et al., 2013).

claim: BAI1 couples to the small GTPase RhoA, driving late RhoA activation in dendrites coincident with growth arrest.
source: Instead, BAI1 couples to the small GTPase RhoA, driving late RhoA activation in dendrites coincident with growth arrest.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements showing increased RhoA activation at dendrite tips and branch points late in development in control neurons, which is blunted in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 3a-c).

claim: BAI1 loss lowers RhoA activation and uncouples it from dendrite dynamics, causing overgrowth.
source: BAI1 loss lowers RhoA activation and uncouples it from dendrite dynamics, causing overgrowth.
evidence: Supported by data showing that BAI1 Kd eliminates the correlation between RhoA activation at dendrite tips and dendrite growth behavior (Figure 3i).

claim: None of BAI1's known downstream effectors mediates BAI1-dependent growth arrest.
source: None of BAI1's known downstream effectors mediates BAI1-dependent growth arrest.
evidence: Supported by data showing that deletion or mutation of the TEV motif, helical domain, GPCR domain, and proline-rich region all rescue BAI1 Kd-induced dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5a-d,f-h).

claim: BAI1 associates with the Rho-GTPase regulatory protein Bcr late in development.
source: Rather, BAI1 associates with the Rho-GTPase regulatory protein Bcr late in development and stimulates its cryptic RhoA-GEF activity, which functions together with its Rac1-GAP activity to terminate arborization.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing interaction between BAI1 and Bcr at 17 DIV and later, but not earlier (Figure 7a-c).

claim: BAI1 stimulates Bcr's cryptic RhoA-GEF activity.
source: Rather, BAI1 associates with the Rho-GTPase regulatory protein Bcr late in development and stimulates its cryptic RhoA-GEF activity, which functions together with its Rac1-GAP activity to terminate arborization.
evidence: Supported by data showing that BAI1 co-expression enhances Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in Cos-7 cells (Figure 7j,k) and that Bcr overexpression rescues BAI1 Kd-induced dendrite overgrowth (Figure 7d-f).

claim: Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity functions together with its Rac1-GAP activity to terminate arborization.
source: Rather, BAI1 associates with the Rho-GTPase regulatory protein Bcr late in development and stimulates its cryptic RhoA-GEF activity, which functions together with its Rac1-GAP activity to terminate arborization.
evidence: Supported by data showing that both GAP-dead and GEF-dead Bcr mutants fail to rescue dendrite overgrowth in Bcr KO neurons or BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 8).

claim: Dendritic arbor architecture profoundly impacts neuronal connectivity and function.
source: Dendritic arbor architecture profoundly impacts neuronal connectivity and function, and aberrant dendritic morphology characterizes neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about the role of dendritic arbors in neuronal function.

claim: Aberrant dendritic morphology characterizes neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Dendritic arbor architecture profoundly impacts neuronal connectivity and function, and aberrant dendritic morphology characterizes neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic defects in neuropsychiatric disorders (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012).

claim: Arbor morphology controls neuronal availability to inputs.
source: Arbor morphology controls neuronal availability to inputs (Landgraf and Evers, 2005; Lefebvre et al., 2015; Häusser and Mel, 2003) and contributes to input processing (Häusser and Mel, 2003; Grienberger et al., 2015; Henze et al., 1996; London and Häusser, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic arbor function.

claim: Arbor morphology contributes to input processing.
source: Arbor morphology controls neuronal availability to inputs (Landgraf and Evers, 2005; Lefebvre et al., 2015; Häusser and Mel, 2003) and contributes to input processing (Häusser and Mel, 2003; Grienberger et al., 2015; Henze et al., 1996; London and Häusser, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic arbor function.

claim: Arbor malformation or degradation manifests in numerous neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Thus, arbor malformation or degradation manifests in numerous neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on dendritic defects in disease.

claim: Intrinsic genetic programs are important, but insufficient, for instructing neurons to form correct dendrite architecture.
source: Intrinsic genetic programs are important, but insufficient, for instructing neurons to form correct dendrite architecture, and extrinsic signals and signaling pathways must supply critical environmental information (Lefebvre et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic development.

claim: Extrinsic signals and signaling pathways must supply critical environmental information for dendrite architecture.
source: Intrinsic genetic programs are important, but insufficient, for instructing neurons to form correct dendrite architecture, and extrinsic signals and signaling pathways must supply critical environmental information (Lefebvre et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic development.

claim: Final arbor structure arises from a tension between drivers and restrictors of dendritic growth.
source: Final arbor structure arises from a tension between drivers and restrictors of dendritic growth (Lefebvre et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic development.

claim: Restrictor failure leads to dendritic overgrowth.
source: Restrictor failure leads to dendritic overgrowth, while ectopic restrictor activation causes dendrite retraction.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about dendritic growth regulation.

claim: Ectopic restrictor activation causes dendrite retraction.
source: Restrictor failure leads to dendritic overgrowth, while ectopic restrictor activation causes dendrite retraction.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about dendritic growth regulation.

claim: Many studies have shown alterations in brain size (both macro- and microcephaly) in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly affecting the hippocampus.
source: Many studies have shown alterations in brain size (both macro- and microcephaly) in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly affecting the hippocampus, which functions in spatial learning, memory consolidation, and emotional control (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012; Copf, 2016; Fombonne et al., 1999; Lainhart et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ASD and brain size.

claim: The hippocampus functions in spatial learning, memory consolidation, and emotional control.
source: Many studies have shown alterations in brain size (both macro- and microcephaly) in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly affecting the hippocampus, which functions in spatial learning, memory consolidation, and emotional control (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012; Copf, 2016; Fombonne et al., 1999; Lainhart et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: Dendrites account for at least 30–40% of gray matter volume.
source: Dendrites account for at least 30–40% of gray matter volume (Curran et al., 2017; Karbowski, 2015; Kasthuri et al., 2015), so defects in arbor size could contribute to such brain defects.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on brain composition.

claim: Defects in arbor size could contribute to brain size defects in ASD.
source: Dendrites account for at least 30–40% of gray matter volume (Curran et al., 2017; Karbowski, 2015; Kasthuri et al., 2015), so defects in arbor size could contribute to such brain defects.
evidence: Inferred from the large contribution of dendrites to gray matter volume.

claim: Dendritic hypertrophy is observed in the hippocampi of mouse models of ASD.
source: Indeed, dendritic hypertrophy is observed in the hippocampi of mouse models of ASD (Cheng et al., 2017; Kwon et al., 2006), and dendritic hypotrophy characterizes other forms of ASD (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012; Kweon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ASD mouse models.

claim: Dendritic hypotrophy characterizes other forms of ASD.
source: Indeed, dendritic hypertrophy is observed in the hippocampi of mouse models of ASD (Cheng et al., 2017; Kwon et al., 2006), and dendritic hypotrophy characterizes other forms of ASD (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012; Kweon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ASD.

claim: Humans and mice suffering from chronic stress, depression/depressive-like behavior, or neurodegenerative disease exhibit dendritic hypotrophy.
source: Further, humans and mice suffering from chronic stress, depression/depressive-like behavior, or neurodegenerative disease exhibit dendritic hypotrophy (Kulkarni and Firestein, 2012; de Flores et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dendritic changes in disease.

claim: ASD-associated macrocephaly manifests well after birth.
source: ASD-associated macrocephaly manifests well after birth (Lainhart et al., 1997; Stigler et al., 2011), which implicates the dysfunction of late-acting dendrite restriction mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ASD macrocephaly.

claim: The late manifestation of ASD-associated macrocephaly implicates the dysfunction of late-acting dendrite restriction mechanisms.
source: ASD-associated macrocephaly manifests well after birth (Lainhart et al., 1997; Stigler et al., 2011), which implicates the dysfunction of late-acting dendrite restriction mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of macrocephaly manifestation.

claim: Little is known about the events whereby neurons in the hippocampus make the transition from growth to stability.
source: While recent work has begun to illuminate the molecular nature of the stable state of dendrites subsequent to growth (Kerrisk et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013), little is known about the events whereby neurons in the hippocampus make this transition.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature and the lack of comprehensive understanding.

claim: The small GTPase Rem2 contributes to a pathway that acts as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth during early postnatal development.
source: The small GTPase Rem2 (Ghiretti et al., 2013), the leucine-rich repeat protein Lrig1 (Alsina et al., 2016), and the adhesion-GPCR (A-GPCR) CELSR3 (Shima et al., 2007) all contribute to apparently separate pathways that act as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth in response to various stimuli during early postnatal development, but almost nothing is known about how these neurons transition out of a net growth state to the more mature, stable state.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Rem2.

claim: The leucine-rich repeat protein Lrig1 contributes to a pathway that acts as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth during early postnatal development.
source: The small GTPase Rem2 (Ghiretti et al., 2013), the leucine-rich repeat protein Lrig1 (Alsina et al., 2016), and the adhesion-GPCR (A-GPCR) CELSR3 (Shima et al., 2007) all contribute to apparently separate pathways that act as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth in response to various stimuli during early postnatal development, but almost nothing is known about how these neurons transition out of a net growth state to the more mature, stable state.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Lrig1.

claim: The adhesion-GPCR CELSR3 contributes to a pathway that acts as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth during early postnatal development.
source: The small GTPase Rem2 (Ghiretti et al., 2013), the leucine-rich repeat protein Lrig1 (Alsina et al., 2016), and the adhesion-GPCR (A-GPCR) CELSR3 (Shima et al., 2007) all contribute to apparently separate pathways that act as a brake on hippocampal dendrite growth in response to various stimuli during early postnatal development, but almost nothing is known about how these neurons transition out of a net growth state to the more mature, stable state.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on CELSR3.

claim: BAI1 instigates phagocytosis of apoptotic cells and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Brain-specific angiogenesis inhibitor 1 (BAI1, also ADGRB1(28)) is an A-GPCR that instigates phagocytosis of apoptotic cells and Gram-negative bacteria (Das et al., 2011; Elliott et al., 2010; Park et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on BAI1 function.

claim: BAI1 is expressed in the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, and thalamus in neurons and glia.
source: BAI1 is expressed in the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, and thalamus in neurons and glia (Sokolowski et al., 2011) and suppresses brain angiogenesis (Kaur et al., 2005), its loss promoting glioblastoma (Koh et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 expression.

claim: BAI1 suppresses brain angiogenesis.
source: BAI1 is expressed in the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, and thalamus in neurons and glia (Sokolowski et al., 2011) and suppresses brain angiogenesis (Kaur et al., 2005), its loss promoting glioblastoma (Koh et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 function.

claim: BAI1 loss promotes glioblastoma.
source: BAI1 is expressed in the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, and thalamus in neurons and glia (Sokolowski et al., 2011) and suppresses brain angiogenesis (Kaur et al., 2005), its loss promoting glioblastoma (Koh et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on BAI1 and glioblastoma.

claim: BAI1 regulates dendritic spine formation, excitatory synaptogenesis and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus and cortex.
source: BAI1 also regulates dendritic spine formation, excitatory synaptogenesis and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus and cortex (Duman et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on BAI1 function in synapses.

claim: BAI1 promotes spino- and synaptogenesis by recruiting the Par3/Tiam1 polarity complex to spines, resulting in localized activation of Rac1 and actin cytoskeletal remodeling.
source: We demonstrated that BAI1 promotes spino- and synaptogenesis by recruiting the Par3/Tiam1 polarity complex to spines, resulting in localized activation of the small GTPase Rac1 and actin cytoskeletal remodeling (Duman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: BAI1 functionally interacts with the ASD-associated synaptic organizer Neuroligin-1, and coordinates trans-synaptic signaling important for excitatory synaptogenesis.
source: Moreover, we recently reported that BAI1 functionally interacts with the ASD-associated synaptic organizer Neuroligin-1, and coordinates trans-synaptic signaling important for excitatory synaptogenesis (Tu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work by the authors.

claim: The BAI1 gene is located in a hot spot for de novo germline mutations in human ASD patients.
source: Notably, the BAI1 gene is located in a hot spot for de novo germline mutations in human ASD patients (Michaelson et al., 2012), and BAI1 SNPs associate with educational attainment and mathematical ability (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 and ASD.

claim: BAI1 SNPs associate with educational attainment and mathematical ability.
source: Notably, the BAI1 gene is located in a hot spot for de novo germline mutations in human ASD patients (Michaelson et al., 2012), and BAI1 SNPs associate with educational attainment and mathematical ability (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 SNPs.

claim: BAI1 mRNA is elevated in mouse models of Rett and MeCP2 duplication syndromes.
source: Moreover, BAI1 mRNA is elevated in mouse models of Rett and MeCP2 duplication syndromes, both of which exhibit altered dendritic arbors and ASD-like symptoms (Chahrour et al., 2008; Urdinguio et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on BAI1 expression in disease models.

claim: Rett and MeCP2 duplication syndromes exhibit altered dendritic arbors and ASD-like symptoms.
source: Moreover, BAI1 mRNA is elevated in mouse models of Rett and MeCP2 duplication syndromes, both of which exhibit altered dendritic arbors and ASD-like symptoms (Chahrour et al., 2008; Urdinguio et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on these syndromes.

claim: BAI1 functions to restrict the growth of dendritic arbors in hippocampal pyramidal cells.
source: We report here that BAI1 also functions to restrict the growth of dendritic arbors in hippocampal pyramidal cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing dendrite overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figures 1-2).

claim: BAI1-mediated restriction of dendritic growth happens late in development as dendritic arbors transition from growth to stabilization.
source: This restriction happens late in development as dendritic arbors transition from growth to stabilization.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal imaging data showing timing of effects (Figure 2).

claim: The shRNA against Adgrb1 lowered BAI1 expression in neuronal somata to undetectable levels.
source: The shRNA lowered BAI1 expression in neuronal somata to undetectable levels, but spared non-transfected cells (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The dorsolateral hippocampal CA1 region exhibited a striking increase in dendrite density in BAI1 knockdown brains relative to controls.
source: The dorsolateral hippocampal CA1 region exhibited a striking increase in dendrite density in BAI1 knockdown (Kd) brains relative to controls, though transfection levels were similar (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 1b.

claim: BAI1 Kd resulted in longer arbors relative to controls.
source: We reconstructed the dendritic arbors of neurons whose somata resided in the center of 100 µm slices cut from control (Figure 1c) and BAI1 Kd (Figure 1d) brains, revealing that BAI1 Kd resulted in longer arbors (Figure 1e), increased dendrite number (Figure 1f), and increased branch points (Figure 1g) relative to controls.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: BAI1 Kd resulted in increased dendrite number relative to controls.
source: We reconstructed the dendritic arbors of neurons whose somata resided in the center of 100 µm slices cut from control (Figure 1c) and BAI1 Kd (Figure 1d) brains, revealing that BAI1 Kd resulted in longer arbors (Figure 1e), increased dendrite number (Figure 1f), and increased branch points (Figure 1g) relative to controls.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: BAI1 Kd resulted in increased branch points relative to controls.
source: We reconstructed the dendritic arbors of neurons whose somata resided in the center of 100 µm slices cut from control (Figure 1c) and BAI1 Kd (Figure 1d) brains, revealing that BAI1 Kd resulted in longer arbors (Figure 1e), increased dendrite number (Figure 1f), and increased branch points (Figure 1g) relative to controls.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: BAI1 Kd arbors showed no excess dorsoventral penetration, indicating that they were still subject to hippocampal boundaries.
source: Though BAI1 Kd arbors overgrew, they showed no excess dorsoventral penetration (Figure 1h), indicating that they were still subject to hippocampal boundaries.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The effects of BAI1 Kd were apparent in both apical and basal dendrites.
source: The effects of BAI1 Kd were apparent in both apical and basal dendrites (Figure 1e–g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b), though apical dendrites showed greater sensitivity to BAI1 loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1e-g and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Apical dendrites showed greater sensitivity to BAI1 loss than basal dendrites.
source: The effects of BAI1 Kd were apparent in both apical and basal dendrites (Figure 1e–g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b), though apical dendrites showed greater sensitivity to BAI1 loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Defects in the orientation of primary apical dendrites were observed in BAI1 Kd neurons.
source: We also observed defects in the orientation of primary apical dendrites from BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d,e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d,e.

claim: Sparse in vivo loss of BAI1 expression causes striking mis- and overgrowth of hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendritic arbors.
source: Thus, sparse in vivo loss of BAI1 expression causes striking mis- and overgrowth of hippocampal pyramidal neuron dendritic arbors.
evidence: Supported by in vivo data from in utero electroporation experiments (Figure 1).

claim: BAI1 Kd in cultured hippocampal neurons reproduced the in vivo effects of BAI1 Kd.
source: Thus, BAI1 Kd with either of two shRNAs in cultured hippocampal neurons reproduced the in vivo effects of BAI1 Kd.
evidence: Supported by data from cultured neurons showing similar phenotypes to in vivo (Figure 1i-k, Figure 1—figure supplement 2f-j).

claim: Some loss of BAI1 was apparent in BAI1 Kd neurons by 10 DIV, becoming complete at 14 DIV and persisting though at least 21 DIV.
source: Some loss of BAI1 was apparent in BAI1 Kd neurons by 10 DIV, becoming complete at 14 DIV and persisting though at least 21 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Significant arbor growth occurred in all neurons between 10 and 17 DIV.
source: Significant arbor growth occurred in all neurons between 10 and 17 DIV; however, control neurons stopped growing at 17 DIV, while BAI1 Kd neurons continued to grow through at least 21 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: Control neurons stopped growing at 17 DIV, while BAI1 Kd neurons continued to grow through at least 21 DIV.
source: Significant arbor growth occurred in all neurons between 10 and 17 DIV; however, control neurons stopped growing at 17 DIV, while BAI1 Kd neurons continued to grow through at least 21 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: At 10 DIV, BAI1 Kd neurons had fewer and shorter dendrites than controls, but they surpassed control neurons in dendrite tip number by DIV 14 and in length by 17 DIV.
source: At 10 DIV, BAI1 Kd neurons had fewer and shorter dendrites than controls, but they surpassed control neurons in dendrite tip number by DIV 14 and in length by 17 DIV (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal imaging data shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: Branch formations and eliminations decreased over the 10–22 DIV time course in control and BAI1 Kd neurons, but more slowly in BAI1 Kd neurons.
source: Branch formations and eliminations decreased over the 10–22 DIV time course in control and BAI1 Kd neurons, but more slowly in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 2a,d,e).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data on branch dynamics shown in Figure 2a,d,e.

claim: BAI1 loss removes a late-acting brake on arbor development, leading to longer, more branched, and less stable dendritic arbors.
source: These data show that BAI1 loss removes a late-acting brake on arbor development, leading to longer, more branched, and less stable dendritic arbors.
evidence: Inferred from the longitudinal data showing continued growth and increased branch dynamics in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 2).

claim: BAI1 OX and control neurons exhibited similar length, dendrite and branch number, and integrated Sholl crossings at 17 DIV.
source: BAI1 OX and control neurons exhibited similar length, dendrite and branch number, and integrated Sholl crossings at 17 DIV, and these parameters remained fairly constant at 21 DIV in control neurons (Figure 2f–j).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2f-j.

claim: All morphological parameters decreased by 21 DIV in BAI1 OX neurons.
source: In contrast, all of these parameters had decreased by 21 DIV in BAI1 OX neurons (Figure 2f–j).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data shown in Figure 2f-j.

claim: BAI1 OX neurons exhibited one more primary dendrite than control neurons at 17 DIV that disappeared by 21 DIV.
source: Additionally, BAI1 OX neurons exhibited one more primary dendrite than control neurons at 17 DIV that disappeared by 21 DIV (Figure 2f,k).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2f,k.

claim: Branch formation and elimination was essentially balanced in control neurons from 17 to 21 DIV, whereas BAI1 OX decreased branch formation and increased branch elimination.
source: In agreement with the data in Figure 2d–e, branch formation and elimination was essentially balanced in control neurons from 17 to 21 DIV, whereas BAI1 OX decreased branch formation and increased branch elimination (Figure 2f,l).
evidence: Supported by data on branch dynamics shown in Figure 2f,l.

claim: BAI1 mediates the transition from arbor growth to termination and arbor stabilization.
source: Taken together, Figures 1–2 suggest that BAI1 mediates the transition from arbor growth to termination and arbor stabilization.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing BAI1 Kd causes continued growth and BAI1 OX causes retraction (Figures 1-2).

claim: Control neurons exhibited a marked increase in RhoA activation at dendrite tips late in development.
source: Strikingly, control neurons exhibited a marked increase in RhoA activation at dendrite tips (Figure 3a,b) and branch points (Figure 3a,c) late in development.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: Control neurons exhibited a marked increase in RhoA activation at branch points late in development.
source: Strikingly, control neurons exhibited a marked increase in RhoA activation at dendrite tips (Figure 3a,b) and branch points (Figure 3a,c) late in development.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 3a,c.

claim: BAI1 Kd neurons showed blunted and delayed RhoA activation at the end of the 15–23 DIV developmental window.
source: BAI1 Kd neurons, by contrast, showed blunted and delayed RhoA activation at the end of the 15–23 DIV developmental window (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 3a-c.

claim: BAI1 mediates a heretofore-undescribed late RhoA activation accompanying dendritic growth arrest.
source: These data reveal that BAI1 mediates a heretofore-undescribed late RhoA activation accompanying dendritic growth arrest.
evidence: Inferred from the FRET data showing late RhoA activation in control neurons that is blunted in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 3a-c).

claim: RhoA KO neurons exhibited increased arbor size and complexity relative to controls late in development (19 DIV).
source: These experiments revealed that RhoA KO neurons exhibited increased arbor size and complexity relative to controls late in development (19 DIV) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–e).
evidence: Supported by data from RhoA KO neurons shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-e.

claim: In control neurons, RhoA activation correlated strikingly with individual dendrite behavior: extending dendrites showed low levels of RhoA activation, while retracting dendrites had high levels thereof.
source: In control neurons, RhoA activation correlated strikingly with individual dendrite behavior (Figure 3e,g,h): extending dendrites showed low levels of RhoA activation, while retracting dendrites had high levels thereof.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3e,g,h.

claim: These differences in RhoA activation were persistent throughout the time course and especially pronounced at the dendrite tips.
source: These differences in RhoA activation were persistent throughout the time course and especially pronounced at the dendrite tips (Figure 3g, left), though also apparent at branch points (Figure 3h, left).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3g,h.

claim: BAI1 Kd profoundly affected the relationship between RhoA activation and dendrite behavior.
source: BAI1 Kd profoundly affected these phenomena. BAI1 Kd neurons had lower RhoA activation levels throughout the time course (Figure 3f–h, right).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3f-h.

claim: At dendrite tips, there was no difference in RhoA activation between extending and retracting dendrites in BAI1 Kd neurons.
source: At dendrite tips, which were the best indicators of dendrite behavior in control neurons, there was no difference in RhoA activation between extending and retracting dendrites in BAI Kd neurons (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: RhoA activation levels at dendrite tips strongly and negatively correlated with dendrite growth in control neurons.
source: The best match was shown in Figure 3i, wherein RhoA activation levels at dendrite tips strongly and negatively correlated with dendrite growth.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claim: BAI1 Kd completely eliminated the correlation between RhoA activation at dendrite tips and dendrite growth.
source: BAI1 Kd, however, completely eliminated this correlation (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claim: RhoA activation at dendritic tips is the primary driver of dendritic retraction in wild type neurons.
source: These data suggest that RhoA activation at dendritic tips is the primary driver of dendritic retraction in wild type neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the strong negative correlation between RhoA activation at tips and dendrite growth (Figure 3i).

claim: Narciclasine activates RhoA in neurons.
source: We first confirmed that narciclasine activated RhoA in neurons by treating Raichu-RhoA-expressing hippocampal neurons with vehicle or 10 nM narciclasine. Narciclasine-treated neurons exhibited increased RhoA activation throughout the dendritic arbor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Low dose narciclasine had no effect on the morphology of control neurons assayed on 21 DIV, but prevented BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth.
source: We therefore applied narciclasine to 17 DIV neurons and found that this low dose of narciclasine had no effect on the morphology of control neurons assayed on 21 DIV, but prevented BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth with respect to dendrite length (Figure 4a,b), dendrite number (Figure 4a,c), branch points (Figure 4a,d), and Sholl curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 4a-d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: Narciclasine had no effect on primary dendrite number.
source: Like BAI1 Kd, narciclasine had no effect on primary dendrite number (Figure 4a,e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a,e.

claim: BAI1 Kd caused decreases in spine density.
source: As we have previously reported, BAI1 Kd caused decreases in spine density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b) and maximum diameter (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,e), but increases in filopod density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,c) and spine length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,d).
evidence: Supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Narciclasine did not rescue the spine density defects caused by BAI1 Kd.
source: Unlike dendritic arbor morphology, narciclasine did not rescue the spine density defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b), though it did block increases in spine length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,d) and decreased spine maximum diameter by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,e), consistent with known effects of RhoA on spine morphology (Tolias et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Y-27632 rescued dendritic arbors from the contraction caused by BAI1 OX.
source: As above, BAI1 OX led to lower total dendrite length (Figure 4f,g), fewer dendrites (Figure 4f,h), fewer branch points (Figure 4f,i), and contracted Sholl curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f,g). All of these effects were prevented by Y-27632 (Figure 4f–i, Figure 4—figure supplement 1f–g).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 4f-i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-g.

claim: Y-27632 did not affect the number of primary dendrites.
source: Y-27632 did not affect the number of primary dendrites (Figure 4f,j).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4f,j.

claim: Modulating RhoA signaling with narciclasine or Y-27632 rescues dendritic arbors from the effects of altered BAI1 signals.
source: Thus, modulating RhoA signaling with narciclasine (RhoA activation) or Y-27632 (ROCK inhibition) rescues dendritic arbors from the effects of altered BAI1 signals, suggesting a role for RhoA signaling downstream of BAI1.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments with narciclasine and Y-27632 (Figure 4).

claim: Deletion or mutation of the TEV motif, helical domain, GPCR domain, and proline-rich region resulted in well-expressed mutants that are surface-localized and capable of rescuing BAI1 Kd-induced increases in dendrite length, number, and branches as effectively as wild-type BAI1.
source: Deletion or mutation of each of these domains resulted in well-expressed mutants that are surface-localized (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b and Tu et al., 2018) and capable of rescuing BAI1 Kd-induced increases in dendrite length, number, and branches as effectively as wild-type BAI1 (Figure 5a–c,f–h).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5a-c,f-h and surface localization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: The ∆TEV BAI1 mutant rescued arbor growth arrest but does not rescue spine development.
source: It is especially interesting that the ∆TEV BAI1 mutant rescued arbor growth arrest, as it does not rescue spine development (Duman et al., 2013), arguing against BAI1's effect on arbors arising as a secondary effect from its effects on synaptogenesis.
evidence: Supported by data showing ∆TEV rescues dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5a,f-h) and citation to previous work showing it does not rescue spine development.

claim: Suppression of activity did not cause arbor overgrowth in control hippocampal neurons, nor did increasing activity prevent overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons.
source: To further address this point, we demonstrated that suppression of activity did not cause arbor overgrowth in control hippocampal neurons, nor did increasing activity prevent overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h,i).
evidence: Supported by data from activity manipulation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h,i.

claim: Deletion of the proline-rich region rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth.
source: We also deleted a proline-rich region that links BAI1 to the scaffold IRSp53 (Oda et al., 1999), and found that this mutant also rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5d,f–h).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5d,f-h.

claim: Neither BAI1 Kd nor any of the mutants affected primary dendrite number.
source: Neither BAI1 Kd nor any of the mutants affected primary dendrite number (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), and all mutants were expressed at levels comparable to wild-type BAI1 (Figure 5a–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: No previously reported BAI1 signaling modality is necessary for restricting dendrite growth.
source: In sum, no previously reported BAI1 signaling modality is necessary for restricting dendrite growth.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing that deletion of known signaling domains does not prevent rescue of dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5).

claim: BAI1-∆N-term. did not rescue dendritic overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons.
source: However, unlike the other mutants, it did not rescue dendritic overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 5e,f–h).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5e,f-h.

claim: Extracellular ligand binding is likely required for BAI1-mediated arbor growth arrest.
source: Thus, extracellular ligand binding is likely required for BAI1-mediated arbor growth arrest.
evidence: Inferred from the failure of the ∆N-term mutant to rescue dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5e,f-h).

claim: All of the BAI1 mutants that rescued dendrite overgrowth also rescued RhoA activation, while BAI1-∆N-term. failed to rescue both defects.
source: Further, all of the BAI1 mutants that rescued dendrite overgrowth (∆TEV, RKR, ∆GPCR, and ∆PRR) also rescued RhoA activation, while BAI1-∆N-term. failed to rescue both defects (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 6a,b.

claim: BAI1 functions through RhoA to mediate dendritic arbor growth arrest.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that BAI1 functions through RhoA to mediate dendritic arbor growth arrest.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between rescue of dendrite overgrowth and rescue of RhoA activation (Figure 6).

claim: Little or no interaction was detected between BAI1 and Bcr before DIV 17, but the interaction was readily detected at the time of dendritic growth arrest.
source: Interestingly, we detected little or no interaction between BAI1 and Bcr before DIV 17, but the interaction was readily detected at the time of dendritic growth arrest (Figure 7a–c).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a-c.

claim: No interaction was detected between BAI1 and Abr.
source: No interaction was detected between BAI1 and Abr (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: Bcr overexpression balanced BAI1 Kd, giving rise to arbors of normal length and complexity while Abr OX did not.
source: However, Bcr OX balanced BAI1 Kd, giving rise to arbors of normal length and complexity while Abr OX did not (Figure 7d–f).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 7d-f.

claim: The effectiveness of Bcr in causing arbor contraction was blunted by BAI1 loss.
source: Moreover, the effectiveness of Bcr in causing arbor contraction, assayed by the final arbor length as a function of Bcr OX level, was blunted by BAI1 loss (Figure 7g–i).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7g-i.

claim: BAI1 activates Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in neurons.
source: This supports the idea that BAI1 activates Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the functional interaction data showing Bcr rescues BAI1 Kd and BAI1 loss blunts Bcr effectiveness (Figure 7d-i).

claim: No functional interaction with Abr was detected.
source: No such functional interaction with Abr was detected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: Both the biochemical and functional data support a role for Bcr in BAI1 signaling rather than Abr.
source: Thus, both the biochemical and functional data support a role for Bcr in BAI1 signaling rather than Abr.
evidence: Inferred from the combined biochemical and functional data showing BAI1-Bcr interaction and functional rescue (Figure 7).

claim: Bcr activates RhoA in Cos-7 cells.
source: We detected RhoA activation in response to Bcr expression in Cos-7 cells (Figure 7j,k).
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in Cos-7 cells shown in Figure 7j,k.

claim: Co-expression with BAI1 greatly enhanced Bcr RhoA-GEF activity.
source: Moreover, co-expression with BAI1 greatly enhanced Bcr RhoA-GEF activity (Figure 7j,k), despite comparable expression of the proteins in the cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1f), suggesting that BAI1 stimulates this activity.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in Cos-7 cells shown in Figure 7j,k.

claim: Bcr loss caused dendritic overgrowth that was rescued by expression of wild type Bcr.
source: As previously reported (Park et al., 2012), Bcr loss caused dendritic overgrowth that was rescued by expression of wild type Bcr (Figure 8a–c).
evidence: Supported by morphological data from Bcr KO neurons shown in Figure 8a-c.

claim: When the rescue was attempted using mutants of Bcr deficient for either Rac1-GAP or RhoA-GEF activity, neither dendritic length nor dendrite number was rescued.
source: Strikingly, when the rescue was attempted using mutants of Bcr deficient for either Rac1-GAP (as previously reported [Park et al., 2012]) or RhoA-GEF activity, neither dendritic length (Figure 8b) nor dendrite number (Figure 8c) was rescued.
evidence: Supported by morphological data from Bcr KO neurons expressing mutant Bcr shown in Figure 8b,c.

claim: Overexpression of neither Bcr-GAP-dead nor Bcr-GEF-dead mutant rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Overexpression of neither mutant rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth in rat hippocampal neurons assayed by length (Figure 8d,e) or dendrite number (Figure 8d,f).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 8d-f.

claim: BAI1-orchestrated dendrite growth arrest requires RhoA activation by Bcr downstream of BAI1 in concert with the Rac1-GAP activity of Bcr.
source: These results suggest that BAI1-orchestrated dendrite growth arrest requires RhoA activation by Bcr downstream of BAI1 in concert with the Rac1-GAP activity of Bcr.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both GAP and GEF activities of Bcr for rescue (Figure 8).

claim: Dendrite growth arrest requires a great change in the signaling environment within dendrites akin to a state change.
source: This suggests that dendrite growth arrest requires a great change in the signaling environment within dendrites akin to a state change.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both RhoA activation and Rac1 inhibition by Bcr (Figure 8).

claim: BAI1 is enriched in hippocampal dendritic spines.
source: We previously demonstrated that BAI1 is enriched in hippocampal dendritic spines (Duman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: BAI1 was present at branch points at 14, 17, and 21 DIV, but did not vary relative to total dendritic BAI1 staining over this time course.
source: BAI1 was present at branch points at 14, 17, and 21 DIV, but did not vary relative to total dendritic BAI1 staining over this time course (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f.

claim: 14 DIV neurons exhibited little BAI1 staining at the dendritic tips, but clear BAI1 staining appeared by 17 DIV and persisted through at least 21 DIV.
source: 14 DIV neurons exhibited little BAI1 staining at the dendritic tips, but clear BAI1 staining appeared by 17 DIV and persisted through at least 21 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f.

claim: BAI1 is present throughout dendrites and critical growth loci at the time of dendrite growth arrest.
source: Thus, BAI1 is present throughout dendrites and critical growth loci at the time of dendrite growth arrest.
evidence: Inferred from the localization data showing BAI1 at tips and branch points at 17 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f).

claim: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth.
source: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999), but the dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood (see below).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on RhoA function.

claim: The dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood.
source: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999), but the dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood (see below).
evidence: Supported by the lack of comprehensive understanding in the literature.

claim: BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips.
source: Moreover, BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips, which seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
evidence: Supported by FRET data showing lower RhoA activation and loss of correlation with dendrite growth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 3).

claim: RhoA activation at the tips seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
source: Moreover, BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips, which seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
evidence: Inferred from the strong correlation between RhoA activation at tips and dendrite growth in control neurons (Figure 3i).

claim: Bcr-dependent activation of RhoA is not sufficient to cause growth arrest but also requires Bcr-mediated inhibition of Rac1.
source: This Bcr-dependent activation of RhoA, however is not sufficient to cause growth arrest but also requires Bcr-mediated inhibition of the complementary small GTPase Rac1.
evidence: Supported by data showing that both GAP-dead and GEF-dead Bcr mutants fail to rescue dendrite overgrowth (Figure 8).

claim: These results strongly implicate a BAI1-Bcr-RhoA pathway in regulating dendritic volume in the hippocampus.
source: These results strongly implicate a BAI1-Bcr-RhoA pathway in regulating dendritic volume in the hippocampus, which is intriguing, especially given the links between BAI1 and ASD (Michaelson et al., 2012; Chahrour et al., 2008; Urdinguio et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing BAI1 activates RhoA through Bcr to restrict dendrite growth.

claim: BAI1 Kd leads to a loss of dendritic spines and synapses in hippocampal neurons.
source: We previously reported that BAI1 Kd also causes a marked decrease in spine density in both cultured hippocampal neurons and in vivo in CA1 and cortical pyramidal neurons (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018). That BAI1 Kd leads to a loss of dendritic spines and synapses in hippocampal neurons (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018) could be misconstrued as the explanation for the longer arbors reported here.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The effect of BAI1 on dendritic arbors is not a side effect of synapse loss.
source: Thus, we can affirm that the effect of BAI1 on dendritic arbors is not a side effect of synapse loss.
evidence: Supported by data showing ∆TEV rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits, and narciclasine rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits (Figures 4-5).

claim: BAI1's role in restricting arbor growth is independent of its effect on promoting dendritic spinogenesis/synaptogenesis, and is mediated by the activation of RhoA by Bcr.
source: Therefore, we conclude that BAI1's role in restricting arbor growth is independent of its effect on promoting dendritic spinogenesis/synaptogenesis, and is mediated by the activation of RhoA by Bcr.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing independence of arbor and spine effects and the role of RhoA and Bcr.

claim: A recent study characterizing global BAI1 KO mice reported no change in dendritic arbor length or spine density as a result of BAI1 loss.
source: A recent study characterizing global BAI1 KO mice reported no change in dendritic arbor length or spine density as a result of BAI1 loss, though no quantitative dendritic data were presented (Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice.

claim: BAI1 KO mice have decreased hippocampus-based learning, lowered threshold for LTP, LTP in response to LTD-provoking stimuli, and decreased PSD thickness.
source: These animals have diminished hippocampus-based learning, lowered threshold for LTP, LTP in response to LTD-provoking stimuli, and decreased PSD thickness (Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice.

claim: BAI1 KO mice have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95.
source: BAI1 KO mice also have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95, which we also reported in our sparse Kd models (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018), and BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice and previous work by the authors.

claim: BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2.
source: BAI1 KO mice also have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95, which we also reported in our sparse Kd models (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018), and BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 function.

claim: BAI1 may assert its effects by conferring an advantage to synapses and/or a disadvantage to dendrites that express it.
source: Further, BAI1 may assert its effects by conferring an advantage to synapses and/or a disadvantage to dendrites that express it. If this were the case, then global loss of BAI1 would even the playing field and the effects of its loss might be greatly ameliorated.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain differences between global KO and sparse Kd.

claim: Global NL1 KO is associated with essentially no effect on spine or synapse density, but sparse NL1 removal causes dramatically lower spine and synapse densities.
source: While NL1 plays a crucial role in synaptic function, global NL1 KO is associated with essentially no effect on spine or synapse density (Kwon et al., 2012). However, if NL1 is removed from a sparse population of neurons, these neurons exhibit dramatically lower spine and synapse densities (Kwon et al., 2012); conversely, if NL1 is overexpressed sparsely, these neurons display higher spine densities and larger spines (Dahlhaus et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on NL1.

claim: There is a functional interaction between BAI1 and NL1 in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, we recently demonstrated a functional interaction between BAI1 and NL1 in hippocampal neurons (Tu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work by the authors.

claim: BAI1 confers an advantage to synapses and a disadvantage to dendritic branches that express it during development.
source: Based on these considerations, we submit that BAI1 confers an advantage to synapses and a disadvantage to dendritic branches that express it during development. These effects are apparent when BAI1 is overexpressed or knocked down on a background of neurons normally expressing BAI1 in culture or in vivo, but that global removal of BAI1 removes this competitive advantage/disadvantage and makes the effects of BAI1 much less evident.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on comparison with NL1 and differences between global KO and sparse manipulations.

claim: Bcr possesses a Rac1-GAP domain and a RhoA-GEF domain.
source: Bcr possesses multiple functional domains, but its most intriguing feature may be that it possesses a Rac1-GAP domain and a RhoA-GEF domain (Park et al., 2012; Rochelle et al., 2013; Tala et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr structure.

claim: Bcr was previously shown to restrict dendrite development and spinogenesis/synaptogenesis through its Rac1-GAP functionality.
source: Bcr was previously shown to restrict dendrite development and spinogenesis/synaptogenesis through its Rac1-GAP functionality (Um et al., 2014; Park et al., 2012), so the requirement for RhoA-GEF activity was unexpected.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr function.

claim: Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has mostly been described in the context of the p210bcr-abl fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome that is associated with virtually all cases of chronic myeloid leukemia.
source: This activity of Bcr has mostly been described in the context of the p210bcr-abl fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome that is associated with virtually all cases of chronic myeloid leukemia, and activates RhoA and various downstream targets thereof (Rochelle et al., 2013; Tala et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr-Abl.

claim: A physiological role for Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has been suggested in keratinocyte differentiation.
source: A physiological role for Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has been suggested in keratinocyte differentiation, though there is no obvious role for its Rac1-GAP activity in this system (Dubash et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Bcr function.

claim: Bcr must both activate an inhibitor of arborization (RhoA) and inhibit an activator of arborization (Rac1) in order to precipitate arbor growth arrest.
source: Our results indicate that Bcr must both activate an inhibitor of arborization (RhoA) and inhibit an activator of arborization (Rac1) in order to precipitate arbor growth arrest (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by data showing requirement for both GAP and GEF activities (Figure 8).

claim: The arrest signal is very high in magnitude, and perhaps requires multiple inputs.
source: This suggests that the arrest signal is very high in magnitude, and perhaps requires multiple inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both RhoA activation and Rac1 inhibition.

claim: RhoA cycles between a GDP-bound inactive form and a GTP-bound active form.
source: Like all small GTPases, RhoA cycles between a GDP-bound inactive form and a GTP-bound active form (Evers et al., 2000; Ridley, 2006).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about small GTPases and citations.

claim: Activated RhoA generally mediates inhibitory/repulsive processes in the nervous system.
source: Activated RhoA generally mediates inhibitory/repulsive processes in the nervous system (Redmond and Ghosh, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claim: RhoA is widely accepted as a physiological antagonist of dendrite growth in a variety of model systems.
source: While RhoA is widely accepted as a physiological antagonist of dendrite growth in a variety of model systems, the studies on which this notion was built primarily employed dominant negative and constitutively active RhoA mutants (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999) or studied the process at a much earlier stage (Takano et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on RhoA function.

claim: Overexpression of either type of GTPase mutant has great potential for broad-spectrum effects that cannot definitively be attributed to the target Rho-GTPase.
source: We now know that overexpression of either type of GTPase mutant has great potential for broad-spectrum effects that cannot definitively be attributed to the target Rho-GTPase (Schiller, 2006; Vega and Ridley, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on GTPase mutants.

claim: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages.
source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claim: RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus.
source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).

evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claim: Very little is known about the developmental dynamics of RhoA activation in dendrites.
source: In all of these studies, RhoA activation was chiefly assayed using techniques that provide no spatial data (Li et al., 2015; Iida et al., 2007; Kranenburg et al., 1999), so very little is known about the developmental dynamics of RhoA activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature and the lack of comprehensive understanding.

claim: RhoA activation peaks late in development and mediates the transition from dendrite growth to growth arrest.
source: We extended these pioneering results by employing a RhoA knockout model (Mulherkar et al., 2013) and by using RhoA-specific FRET probes (Nakamura et al., 2006; Pertz et al., 2006) to measure authentic RhoA effects and spatiotemporal dynamics. In so doing, we elucidated three previously unknown features of dendritic RhoA signaling: (i) RhoA activation peaks late in development and mediates the transition from dendrite growth to growth arrest; (ii) BAI1 is required to activate RhoA in this context, presumably by transducing some signal and (iii) RhoA activation levels established by 16 DIV determine the ultimate developmental fate of individual persistent dendrites.
evidence: Supported by FRET data showing late RhoA activation peak (Figure 3).

claim: BAI1 is required to activate RhoA in the context of dendrite growth arrest, presumably by transducing some signal.
source: We extended these pioneering results by employing a RhoA knockout model (Mulherkar et al., 2013) and by using RhoA-specific FRET probes (Nakamura et al., 2006; Pertz et al., 2006) to measure authentic RhoA effects and spatiotemporal dynamics. In so doing, we elucidated three previously unknown features of dendritic RhoA signaling: (i) RhoA activation peaks late in development and mediates the transition from dendrite growth to growth arrest; (ii) BAI1 is required to activate RhoA in this context, presumably by transducing some signal and (iii) RhoA activation levels established by 16 DIV determine the ultimate developmental fate of individual persistent dendrites.
evidence: Supported by FRET data showing blunted RhoA activation in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 3).

claim: RhoA activation levels established by 16 DIV determine the ultimate developmental fate of individual persistent dendrites.
source: We extended these pioneering results by employing a RhoA knockout model (Mulherkar et al., 2013) and by using RhoA-specific FRET probes (Nakamura et al., 2006; Pertz et al., 2006) to measure authentic RhoA effects and spatiotemporal dynamics. In so doing, we elucidated three previously unknown features of dendritic RhoA signaling: (i) RhoA activation peaks late in development and mediates the transition from dendrite growth to growth arrest; (ii) BAI1 is required to activate RhoA in this context, presumably by transducing some signal and (iii) RhoA activation levels established by 16 DIV determine the ultimate developmental fate of individual persistent dendrites.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data showing persistent differences in RhoA activation between extending and retracting dendrites (Figure 3e-h).

claim: These results provide a bridge between the expansion of dendritic arbors during development and the requirement for RhoA inhibition to achieve dendrite stability at later time points.
source: These results provide a bridge between the expansion of dendritic arbors during development and the requirement for RhoA inhibition to achieve dendrite stability at later time points (Lin et al., 2013; Sfakianos et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from the data showing RhoA activation during growth arrest and citations to literature on RhoA inhibition for stability.

claim: Narciclasine is effective on RhoA at very low concentrations.
source: We used narciclasine to activate RhoA late in development. Though narciclasine is effective on RhoA at very low concentrations (Fürst, 2016; Lefranc et al., 2009; Van Goietsenoven et al., 2013), it has other targets, including ef1A (Fürst, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on narciclasine.

claim: Narciclasine has marked cytotoxic effects at concentrations at 1 µM, though at 50 nM it has a cytostatic effect due to its action on the cytoskeleton though RhoA.
source: Narciclasine has marked cytotoxic effects at concentrations at 1 µM, though at 50 nM it has a cytostatic effect, and this is due to its action on the cytoskeleton though RhoA (Van Goietsenoven et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on narciclasine.

claim: Narciclasine at 10 nM activated RhoA and had no effect on Rac1 at 20 nM.
source: We observed effective activation of RhoA at 10 nM, and it had no effect on Rac1 at twice the concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Y-27632 inhibits several kinases but is most effective on those regulated by RhoA.
source: We also acknowledge a lack of specificity of Y-27632 and note that although it inhibits several kinases, it is most effective on those regulated by RhoA (Davies et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Y-27632.

claim: At the concentrations used, there was no effect of either narciclasine or Y-27632 on control neurons.
source: At the concentrations that we use, there was no effect of either drug on the control neurons.
